sentences.text: Valdosaurus canaliculatus is the only valid species of this bipedal, herbivorous dryosaurid dinosaur, which belongs to the family Dryosauridae within the class Ornithischia.

The holotype femurs belonged to a juvenile individual, while an adult would be a medium-sized euornithopod with femurs reaching half a meter in length, and the newly described specimen would have measured around 4 to 5 meters in length.
While type specimens were small, reaching only 10 kilograms in mass, larger individuals like the Compton Bay find may have weighed as much as 400 kilograms.
Valdosaurus caudal vertebrae have lengthened, backswept neural spines that overhang more than one following vertebra, a trait distinct from other ornithischians.
Unlike other dryosaurids, Valdosaurus canaliculatus has an open obturator notch on the pubis.
Rev. William Fox collected two small femora near Cowleaze Chine on the Isle of Wight in the 19th century, a site on the southwest coast of the island.

In 1889, Richard Lydekker assigned the remains to Camptosaurus valdensis based on a partial lower jaw and other bones, but in 1975 Peter Galton assigned the femora to Dryosaurus canaliculatus after concluding they did not belong to Camptosaurus, and Peter Galton created the new genus Valdosaurus for this species in 1977.
Galton and Philippe Taquet described a second species, V. nigeriensis, from Niger in 1982.
In 2009, Peter Galton concluded that fossils from outside England could not be reliably assigned to Valdosaurus and reclassified V. nigeriensis as Elrhazosaurus.
Nick Chase discovered a new Valdosaurus specimen in Compton Bay on the Isle of Wight in 2012, with the exact location withheld to prevent theft.
Sedimentological data suggests the depositional environment of the Wessex Formation was a floodplain intersected by river and lake deposits.
Burned plant and insect material and fusain suggest that the environment experienced frequent wildfires.

Valdosaurus lived during the Early Cretaceous, approximately between 130 and 125 million years ago in the Barremian stage, in what is now Europe, where fossils have been found on the Isle of Wight and other parts of England, and the rock units where Valdosaurus fossils were found were deposited between the Berriasian and Barremian, approximately 145 to 125 million years ago.

It is debated whether many English specimens, including cranial elements and teeth, truly belong to Valdosaurus, and it is uncertain whether many of the English specimens truly belong to Valdosaurus, including all cranial material and teeth.
The presence of Valdosaurus in Spain remains questionable.
